notes.text: てもいい is "even if you do, it's fine". As a question, ～てもいいですか asks "may I?", and the answer is often just いいですよ. Friends say ～てもいい？
てはいけない is "if you do, it won't do": it isn't allowed. Politely it's ～てはいけません. Friends often just say だめ, no.

grammar.title: ～ないで / ～ないでください
grammar.summary: A verb's ない form plus で asks someone not to do it: 撮らないでください, please don't take pictures. In the middle of a sentence it means "without": 食べないで来た, came without eating.
grammar.body:
写真を撮らないでください。
朝、食べないで会社に来ました。
translations: I came to work without eating this morning.

notes.text: ないでください is the negative of ～てください: 撮ってください, please take one; 撮らないでください, please don't. Friends drop ください: 撮らないで！
In the middle of a sentence, ～ないで says how the next thing was done: without doing this one, or instead of it.

grammar.title: ～える / ～られる
grammar.summary: The potential form says what you can do: 歌う (sing), 歌える (can sing); 出る (go out, take part), 出られる (can take part).
grammar.body:
新しいバンドも、出られる？
ユキさん、歌えるじゃん！
明日は行けない。

notes.text: う verbs change their last sound to the え row and add る: 行く, 行ける; 歌う, 歌える. る verbs take られる: 出る, 出られる. In speech that's often just れる: 出れる.
The new verb changes like a る verb: 行けない (can't go), 歌えた (could sing). 来る becomes 来れる, and する becomes できる, which you know already.

grammar.title: ～たら
grammar.summary: ら on a verb's past form says "if" or "when": 勝ったら, if we win. It's the everyday way to say "if".
grammar.body:
もし勝ったら、どうする？
雨が降ったら、どうする？
負けたら、また来年。
練習が終わったら、ラーメン食べよう。
translations: What do we do if we win?
If we lose, there's next year.
Let's have ramen once practice is over.

notes.text: Take the plain past and add ら: 勝った, 勝ったら; 降った, 降ったら. Then say what happens. もし (if) in front is optional; it flags early that an "if" is coming.
It works on any past form: 負けなかったら (if we don't lose), 出られたら (if we can get in), 暑かったら (if it's hot), 雨だったら (if it's rain).
For something sure to happen, たら means "when" or "once": 終わったら, when it's over.

grammar.title: ～なきゃ / ～なくてもいい
grammar.summary: なきゃいけない or なくちゃ on a verb's ない stem says you have to: 練習しなくちゃ, I have to practise. なくてもいい says you don't: 緊張しなくてもいい, no need to be nervous.
grammar.body:
練習しなくちゃ。
動画を送らなきゃいけない。
新しい曲じゃなくてもいい。
translations: We have to send a video.
It doesn't have to be a new song.

notes.text: Take the ない form and swap ない for なくちゃ: 練習しない, 練習しなくちゃ. It's short for なくては (いけない): "if I don't, it won't do".
なきゃ is short for なければ, "if not", and does the same job. Friends often drop the いけない. In writing and formal talk it's the whole なければならない.
なくてもいい is the other way round: even not doing it is fine. After a noun it's じゃなくてもいい.

grammar.title: ～くなる / ～になる / ～く
grammar.summary: なる means become: 暑くなる, get hot; 上手になる, get good. An adjective's く form on its own says how something's done: 大きく歌う, sing out loud.
grammar.body:
夏が、暑くなった。
歌が、上手になった。
今は、大きく歌える。
translations: Now I can sing out loud.

notes.text: An i-adjective swaps its い for く before なる: 暑い, 暑くなる. いい becomes よくなる.
A noun or a na-adjective takes に: 上手になる, 静かになる, 一つになる.
The same く form, with no なる after it, tells how something's done: 大きく (big, loud), 楽しく (happily), うまく (well).

grammar.title: ～みたい / ～そう
grammar.summary: みたい after a noun or a plain verb says it seems so: 雨みたい, sounds like rain. そう on an adjective's stem says how it looks: 怖そう, she looks scary.
grammar.body:
雨みたい。
リン、怒ってるみたい。
リンさん、ちょっと怖そう。

notes.text: みたい is a guess from what you see or hear. It goes straight after a noun, or after the plain form of a verb or adjective: 怒ってるみたい, she seems angry.
Before a noun it's みたいな: 雨みたいな曲, a song like rain. In writing and formal talk it's ～ようだ.
そう goes on an adjective with its い dropped (怖い, 怖そう; 楽しい, 楽しそう) or on a verb's stem. It's how something looks to you, before you know. いい becomes よさそう.

grammar.title: ～ちゃう / ～てしまう
grammar.summary: しまう after a verb's て form says it's done and over, often when you didn't want it: 切れてしまった, it went and snapped. Friends say ちゃう: 切れちゃった.
grammar.body:
切れちゃった。
歌、忘れちゃった。
私、緊張しちゃう。

notes.text: て plus しまう shrinks to ちゃう, and で plus しまう to じゃう: 忘れちゃう, 飲んじゃう. In the past, ちゃった and じゃった.
It's often a small "oops": it happened, and it can't be undone. It can also just say something's done completely, or can't be helped.
The full てしまう is for writing and polite talk: 切れてしまいました.

grammar.title: ～てみる
grammar.summary: みる after a verb's て form means do it and see how it goes: 歌ってみる, try singing it.
grammar.body:
歌ってみて。
言葉、書いてみた。
もう一回、やってみよう。

notes.text: It's the verb 見る (see), written in kana: do something, and see what happens.
みる changes like 見る: やってみた (I tried it), やってみよう (let's give it a go), 静かにしてみて (try it quieter).

grammar.title: だけ / しか
grammar.summary: だけ after a word means only that: 三曲だけ, just three songs. しか with a negative verb means the same, with a feeling of not enough: 三曲しかない, we've only got three songs.
grammar.body:
三曲しかない。
三曲だけ。
ステージは、一回だけ。
translations: We only get one go on the stage.

notes.text: しか always comes with a negative: しかない (there's only), しか知らない (only know). It says there should be more.
だけ just says that's all there is, with no complaint, and works with any verb: 一回だけ (only once), 俺だけ (only me).
それだけ, "that's all", ends what you have to say.

grammar.title: ～に行く / へ
grammar.summary: に after a verb's stem says what you're going or coming for: 見に行く, go to see; 見せに来た, came to show. へ marks where you're headed, much like に: スタジオへ行く.
grammar.body:
ラーメンを食べに行こう。
ユキに見せに来た。
スタジオへ行った。

notes.text: Take a verb's ます stem (食べます, 食べ), add に, then a verb of going: 行く, 来る or 帰る. The に says what the trip is for.
A する verb's stem is し: 練習しに行く, go to practise. 何しに来たの？ asks what someone came for.
へ is the kana he, but read え. It points toward a place, and with 行く and 来る it does the same job as に.

grammar.title: より / ～のほうが
grammar.summary: より marks what you compare against: 私の絵より, than my drawing. のほうが picks the side that's more so: プロのほうが上手, the pro's better.
grammar.body:
プロの絵は、私の絵よりきれい。
プロのほうが、上手。
春より、上手になった。
translations: The pro's drawing is cleaner than mine.

notes.text: A は B より, then an adjective: A is more so than B. There's no word for "more"; the adjective does the work.
ほう means side. A noun takes の before it (プロのほう), a verb doesn't (勝つほう). が marks it as the one that's more so.
To ask which of two, say どっち: どっちがいい？, which is better? The answer often has のほうが, and sometimes より too.

grammar.title: ～とき
grammar.summary: とき after a verb, an adjective, or a noun with の says when something happens: 行くとき, when I go; 子供のとき, when I was a kid.
grammar.body:
仕事に行くとき、いつも歌を聞く。
子供のとき、毎日マンガを読んでいた。
ユキのバンドを見たとき、すごいと思った。
translations: When I go to work, I always listen to music.
When I was a kid, I read manga every day.
When I saw Yuki's band, I thought it was amazing.

notes.text: とき (時) is the word for time. What comes before it says which time: a plain verb, an adjective (忙しいとき, when I'm busy), a na-adjective with な (静かなとき), or a noun with の.
A past verb before とき says it had already happened: 見たとき, when I saw it. A present verb says it hadn't yet, or happens every time.
Compare たら: 見たら leans toward "once I see it" or "if"; 見たとき just says at the time.

grammar.title: ～前に / ～た後で / ～てから
grammar.summary: 前に after a plain verb says before: 寝る前に, before bed. 後で after a past verb says after: 終わった後で, after it's over. から after a verb's て form says after, and then: 食べてから, after eating.
grammar.body:
仕事に行く前に、コーヒーを飲む。
仕事が終わった後で、ラーメンを食べる。
食べてから、行こう。
translations: Before I go to work, I have a coffee.
After work's over, I have ramen.

notes.text: The verb before 前に is always plain present, even in a story told in the past: 寝る前に読んだ, I read before bed.
後で (あとで) goes the other way: the verb before it is always past. On its own, 後で means "later".
～てから puts two things in order: this one, and only then that one. It's the everyday way to say one thing has to come first.

grammar.title: や / ～たり / など
grammar.summary: や lists a few nouns out of more: ラーメンや卵, ramen, eggs and so on. ～たり does the same for things you do: 読んだり、書いたり. など after a list says it goes on.
grammar.body:
休みの日は、マンガを読んだり、ゲームをしたりする。
コンビニで、ビールや水を買った。
マンガやゲームなどが好き。
translations: On my days off I read manga, play games, that kind of thing.
I bought beer, water and stuff at the konbini.
I like manga, games, that sort of thing.

notes.text: Take a verb's past form (読んだ, した) and add り: 読んだり, したり. Give two or so, then する in whatever form the sentence needs: したりする, したりした. In casual talk the last する often drops: 読んだり、書いたり。
や joins nouns like と does, but と gives the whole list, and や only a few of them. ビールと水 is just those two; ビールや水 is those and more.
など after the last one says there's more where that came from. It often closes a list made with や, and can follow just one: ラーメンなど, ramen and the like.

grammar.title: ～の
grammar.summary: の after a verb or adjective makes it something you can talk about like a noun: 歌うのが好き, I like singing; 大きいのを買った, I bought the big one.
grammar.body:
ユキが歌うのが、好き。
ユキが歌うのを、聞いた。
大きいのを買った。
translations: I love it when Yuki sings.

notes.text: A plain verb, then の, and the whole thing works like a noun: it takes が, を, は or も after it. 一人で食べるのは、寂しい: eating alone is lonely.
With 見る and 聞く, the の is what you see or hear going on: 笑うのを見た, I saw her laugh.
After an adjective, の stands for a thing you've already talked about: 大きいの, the big one; 新しいの, the new one. A na-adjective takes な first: 静かなの, the quiet one.

grammar.title: ～てくれる / ～てあげる / ～てもらう
grammar.summary: After a verb's て form, くれる, あげる and もらう say who a favour is for: 作ってくれた, someone made it for me; 作ってあげた, I made it for someone; 作ってもらった, I had someone make it.
grammar.body:
ソラが、コーヒーを入れてくれた。
私が、ソラにコーヒーを入れてあげた。
ケンタに、写真を撮ってもらった。
translations: I got Kenta to take a photo.

notes.text: ～てくれる: someone does something for me, or for my side (my family, my friends, my band). It carries a little thanks.
～てあげる goes the other way: I, or my side, do something for someone else. Said to that person's face it can sound like you're doing them a big favour, so people often say just 入れるよ instead.
～てもらう looks at the same favour from my side: I get it done. The one who does it takes に. Asking for one, people say 撮ってもらってもいい？, could you take it for me?

grammar.title: ～ので / ～し
grammar.summary: ので gives a reason, softer than から: 仕事なので, since I've got work. し adds a reason, hinting there are more: 安いし、うまいし, it's cheap, it's good.
grammar.body:
明日は仕事なので、もう寝る。
店長のラーメンは、安いし、うまいし、最高。
寒いし、もう帰ろう。
translations: I've got work tomorrow, so I'm off to bed.
The manager's ramen is cheap, it's good, it's the best.
It's cold and all, so let's head home.

notes.text: ので goes after a plain verb or adjective: 雨が降っているので, 寒いので. A noun or na-adjective takes な first: 仕事なので, 静かなので. It sounds softer and politer than から, so it's what people use with です and ます: 仕事があるので、行けません。
し after a plain form lists a reason, and leaves room for more. Two in a row make a case for something.
Just one し says "for one thing": the rest go unsaid.

grammar.title: ～のに
grammar.summary: のに joins two things where the second isn't what you'd expect: 練習したのに、うまくできなかった, I practised, and still it didn't go well.
grammar.body:
練習したのに、うまく歌えなかった。
休みなのに、仕事に行った。
見たかったのに。
translations: Even though I practised, I couldn't sing it well.
I went to work even though it was my day off.
And I wanted to see it, too.

notes.text: のに goes after a plain verb or adjective. A noun or na-adjective takes な first: 休みなのに, even though it's a day off. It carries a feeling: surprise, disappointment, sometimes a complaint.
Compare けど: けど just says "but"; のに says it went against what should have happened.
At the end of a sentence, のに is a sigh about what should have been, with the rest left unsaid.

grammar.title: ～ほうがいい / ～すぎる
grammar.summary: ほうがいい gives advice: 寝たほうがいい, you'd better get some sleep. すぎる after a stem says too much: 飲みすぎた, I drank too much.
grammar.body:
今日は、寝たほうがいいよ。
夜、ビールを飲みすぎた。
このラーメン、熱すぎる。
translations: You'd better get some sleep today.
I drank too much beer last night.

notes.text: For doing something, the verb before ほうがいい is usually past: 行ったほうがいい, you should go. For not doing it, use ない: 行かないほうがいい, better not go. It's the ほう of のほうが: of the two ways, this one's better.
すぎる goes on a verb's stem (飲み, 食べ, し) or an adjective without its い (高い, 高すぎる; 静か, 静かすぎる), and changes like 食べる: すぎた, すぎない.
The stem すぎ works as a noun on its own: 飲みすぎ, too much drinking; 練習しすぎ, too much practice.

grammar.title: ～たことがある
grammar.summary: A past verb, then ことがある, says it's happened at least once: 行ったことがある, I've been there. ことがない says never.
grammar.body:
カナダに行ったことがある？
ステージで歌ったことがない。
マンガは、読んだことはある。
translations: Have you ever been to Canada?
I've never sung on a stage.

notes.text: こと is a thing, an event: 行ったこと, the having gone. ある says there's such a thing in your past. Ask with ある？, and answer ある or ない.
ない says never. は or も can take the place of が: 見たことはある, I've seen it, at least; 食べたこともない, I've never even eaten it.
It's about what you've been through, not about today: ラーメンを食べた is what you just did; ラーメンを食べたことがある says you know what it's like.
